title: Unit-Rooted Polynomial
content: A structure packaging a monic polynomial of degree $n$ with all roots in the closed unit disk $\overline{\mathbb{D}}$. Represented as `roots : Fin n → ℂ` with the constraint $|r_i| \le 1$ for all $i$. The polynomial is then $f(z) = \prod_{i=1}^n (z - r_i)$, which is automatically monic of degree $n$.

title: Polynomial Evaluation
content: Evaluates the monic polynomial $f(z) = \prod_{i=1}^n (z - r_i)$ at a point $z \in \mathbb{C}$ using `Finset.prod`. This is the product representation rather than the coefficient representation, which is more natural for studying sublevel sets since the root locations directly determine the geometry of $\{|f(z)| \le 1\}$.

title: Sublevel Set (Lemniscate)
content: The sublevel set $E = \{z \in \mathbb{C} : |f(z)| \le 1\}$, also called a polynomial lemniscate. For $f(z) = z^n$, this is the closed unit disk. For general root configurations, $E$ can be a complicated multiply-connected region with thin passages ('necks') connecting components near clustered roots. The boundary $\{|f(z)| = 1\}$ is a lemniscate curve.

title: Shortest Path Length
content: The infimum of lengths of continuous paths $\gamma : [0,1] \to E$ with $\gamma(0) = 0$ and $|\gamma(1)| = 1$. This captures the shortest way to travel from the origin to the unit circle while staying inside the sublevel set. The Clunie-Netanyahu theorem guarantees the infimum is taken over a nonempty set.

title: Worst-Case Path Length
content: The supremum over all unit-rooted polynomials of degree $n$ of the shortest path length: $W(n) = \sup_f \ell(f)$. This is the quantity Erdos asked about: does $W(n) \to \infty$? The trivial lower bound $W(n) \ge 1$ comes from $f(z) = z^n$, where $E$ is the unit disk and the shortest path is the segment $[0,1]$.

title: f(0) = Product of Negated Roots
content: $f(0) = \prod_{i=1}^n (-r_i)$ and $|f(0)| = \prod_{i=1}^n |r_i|$. Since each $|r_i| \le 1$, we get $|f(0)| \le 1$, so the origin always lies in the sublevel set $E$. This is the starting point of the path problem.

title: Origin Always in E
content: The origin $0$ always belongs to the sublevel set $E$ for any unit-rooted polynomial. This is proved by showing $|f(0)| = \prod |r_i| \le 1$ since each $|r_i| \le 1$. This guarantees the path problem is well-posed: the starting point $0$ is always in $E$.

title: Case f(z) = z^n: Unit Disk
content: When all roots are at the origin ($r_i = 0$), $f(z) = z^n$ and the sublevel set is exactly the closed unit disk $\{|z| \le 1\}$. The proof uses `map_pow` and the equivalence $|z|^n \le 1 \iff |z| \le 1$ (for $n \ge 1$). This is the trivial case where the shortest path has length 1 (the segment $[0,1]$).

title: Degree 1: Shifted Disk
content: For degree 1 with root $r$ ($|r| \le 1$), $f(z) = z - r$ and $E = \{|z - r| \le 1\}$ is a closed disk of radius 1 centered at $r$. The origin is in this disk since $|0 - r| = |r| \le 1$. The shortest path from 0 to the unit circle depends on the position of $r$.

title: Unimodular Roots: |f(0)| = 1
content: When all roots have $|r_i| = 1$ (unimodular/roots on the unit circle), $|f(0)| = \prod |r_i| = 1$. This means 0 is on the boundary of $E$, making the path problem hardest — the origin barely qualifies as a starting point. Unimodular configurations are expected to produce the extremal cases.

title: Erdős Problem #1120: W(n) → ∞
content: The main open conjecture: the worst-case shortest path length $W(n) \to \infty$ as $n \to \infty$. Stated as an axiom: $\forall M \in \mathbb{R},\; \exists N_0$ such that $n \ge N_0 \implies W(n) \ge M$. This captures the idea that high-degree polynomials can create sublevel sets where any path from 0 to the unit circle must be arbitrarily long.

title: Clunie-Netanyahu: Path Always Exists
content: Clunie and Netanyahu proved that for any unit-rooted polynomial of degree $\ge 1$, there exists a continuous path from 0 to the unit circle lying entirely within $E$. This is non-trivial: the sublevel set could a priori be disconnected between 0 and $|z| = 1$. Their result guarantees the path problem is always solvable, making $\ell(f)$ well-defined and finite.

title: Erdős Growth Bound Conjecture
content: Erdos conjectured that $W(n)$ grows slowly — at most linearly: $W(n) \le Cn$ for some constant $C > 0$. Combined with the main conjecture $W(n) \to \infty$, this would pin down the growth as between constants and linear. The slow growth reflects the intuition that polynomial lemniscates, while becoming topologically complex, cannot force paths to be much longer than the degree.
